archetype.name: Fringe Contender (pass-first, takeaway-fueled)
archetype.definition: A new-regime team with a league-average-plus passing offense and a disruptive but leaky defense, whose 3-2 start leans on takeaways and a soft early schedule more than on dominance.

report.headline: Kubiak fixed the passing game; the turnover-fed defense is now coming back to earth.
report.take:
Start with where this came from. The 2025 Raiders went 3-14 with the league's worst offense by EPA (-0.192, 32nd) and 14.2 points a game. Five weeks into Klint Kubiak's first year they score 26.4 a game (9th) and sit 13th in offensive EPA. That is a real structural change, not a fluke. All of it comes through the air: Kirk Cousins has started every game, pass EPA per play is 0.181 (10th), the line keeps him clean enough (4.2% sack rate, 5th), and his game-level pass EPA has climbed almost every week, from 0.4 in the opener to 10.5 at New England. Brock Bowers drew 34 targets in the three games he played, and Ashton Jeanty adds 30 more as a receiver.

The run game is the opposite story. Jeanty has 88 carries behind a line that gives him 1.39 yards before contact, dead last. The team averages 3.12 a carry (30th) with -0.237 EPA per rush (29th), and rushing yards have slid to 72 and then 38 the last two weeks. This isn't game script. Three of those games were wins. The blocking can't move anyone, and the offense is effectively one-dimensional, which caps it in the red zone and on short yardage (50% conversion, 26th).

The 3-0 start hides something. The defense posted 13 and 14 points allowed against Miami and the Chargers, offenses that now rank 30th and 32nd, and it forced nine takeaways in the first three games. Against Kansas City (4th) and New England (11th) it gave up 30 and 45 with one takeaway total, including 374 passing yards to the Patriots. The pass rush is real: a 30.3% pressure rate (2nd) and 20.5% QB hit rate (3rd) don't come from luck. But the coverage behind it is 21st in pass EPA allowed and 29th on short passes. The run defense posts a strong per-play number (6th) while giving up explosive runs at the 31st-ranked rate. The red zone is 29th, allowing touchdowns 77.8% of the time. League-leading takeaways covered a defense that is only average once the ball stays in opponents' hands.

So the honest read is a team with a net EPA just inside the top 12, a +0.6 point differential, and about a win of luck in the record. An 0.8 cover rate says the market has been slow to catch up to the offense. The back half of the schedule is soft, with Tennessee, Arizona and the Chargers twice-adjacent stretch late, so a winning season is plausible. Becoming more than a fringe team requires either a run game or a defense that can hold good offenses without turnovers.

strengths.title: A genuinely rebuilt passing attack
strengths.body: Pass EPA per play sits 10th, a massive jump from an offense that was last in the league a year ago. Cousins' production has risen with the opponents, peaking against KC and NE. The line's low sack rate gives the scheme time. Because it is built on scheme, a stable QB and a deep target tree with Bowers and Jeanty, it should hold up.

strengths.title: Pass rush that lives in the backfield
strengths.body: A 30.3% pressure rate (2nd) and 20.5% hit rate (3rd) are the engine behind the defense's 13 sacks and many of its takeaways. Pressure is one of the stickier defensive traits, so this part of the defense should travel. The takeaway total built on it will not keep its pace.

concerns.title: Defense built on bad offenses, turnovers
concerns.body: The good defensive weeks came against offenses now ranked 30th and 32nd, and 9 of the 10 takeaways came in the first three games. Against KC and NE the unit allowed 75 points and over 370 passing yards in the latest game. With coverage weak underneath and the red zone 29th, this looks like a mid-to-low-tier defense whose takeaway luck is fading.

concerns.title: No run game behind the line
concerns.body: With last-ranked yards before contact and run EPA 29th, Jeanty's volume is mostly wasted carries. The trend is worsening, down to 38 rushing yards at New England. This is a line problem rather than a back problem, and it won't fix itself midseason. It makes the offense predictable near the goal line and in short yardage.

concerns.title: Explosive runs leak through
concerns.body: The run defense wins per play but allows explosive runs at the 31st-ranked rate, a boom-or-bust pattern. Missed tackles (22nd) feed it. Against a backfield that gets downhill, those breakdowns become points.

trend.note: Points allowed have risen every single week (13, 14, 27, 30, 45) as the takeaways dried up and the opponents improved. Meanwhile the passing game kept climbing, so the offense is rising even as results slip.

nextGame.headline: Shootout setup: Raiders' air attack meets Buffalo's broken pass defense
nextGame.body:
Buffalo is the league's best offense by EPA (0.211) paired with its 30th-ranked defense, and it fits the Raiders' profile almost exactly. Cousins' passing game should find room against a defense 29th in pass EPA allowed and 27th on short throws. The Raiders' leaky coverage, though, faces Josh Allen and a run game that leads the league in yards before contact and run success. That run game is aimed straight at a defense that gives up explosive runs. The Raiders' one big edge is their pressure against a Buffalo line that has kept hits on Allen low (5th). Buffalo's -0.8 turnover margin also gives a takeaway-hungry defense real chances.

Availability favors Las Vegas at the margins. Buffalo's most recent report, from its Monday game, listed WRs DJ Moore and Joshua Palmer, DT Ed Oliver, edge Landon Jackson and slot CB Dee Alford out, with RT Spencer Brown hurt mid-game. Those are estimated returns for Sunday, not certainties, but missing Alford would thin an already weak underneath coverage. For the Raiders, rotational DT Tonka Hemingway (52% snaps) is in concussion protocol. WR Jalen Nailor is expected to practice. The backup center is out. Indoors, so no weather factor.

keyMatchups.title: Cousins vs. Buffalo's soft underneath coverage
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo allows 0.256 EPA per dropback and grades poorly on short passes, exactly where Bowers and Jeanty live. Tight ends have been productive against Buffalo per play, though Buffalo funnels fewer targets to them. If Alford sits, the middle of the field gets even softer.

keyMatchups.title: Buffalo's ground game vs. explosive leaks
keyMatchups.body: Buffalo's backs get 3.53 yards before contact, the best in the league, with a run success rate of 51.5%. The Raiders stop runs on a per-play basis but allow too many big ones. The game likely tilts on whether the Raiders' fronts hold up early, especially if Hemingway is out.

keyMatchups.title: Raiders pressure vs. Allen's ball security
keyMatchups.body: The Raiders are second in pressure rate, and Buffalo's turnover margin ranks 25th. Takeaways are the cleanest path for an underdog to steal possessions in a high-total game. If Brown can't go at right tackle, that edge grows.

nextGame.watch: Whether the Raiders' pass rush produces early takeaways off Allen. Without them, this defense has been giving up 30-plus to good offenses.

restOfSeason.body:
The passing offense is the sustainable part. Expect it to stay a top-12 unit and keep the Raiders in most games, with scoring settling around the mid-20s as the schedule toughens through SF and Seattle's defense. The defense's early-season numbers will keep regressing. A league-leading takeaway pace on top of 21st-ranked pass defense doesn't last, and points allowed should sit in the mid-20s, closer to the last two weeks than the first two. The pressure rate should keep it from collapsing entirely.

The schedule is the reason for optimism. After a hard middle stretch (BUF, at SF, SEA), December brings the 0-5 Chargers, 0-5 Titans and 1-4 Cardinals, all with bottom-tier offenses. A 9-8 or 10-7 finish that keeps them in wild-card range is realistic, but with a non-functional run game and a coverage unit exposed by good QBs, they are more likely to be spoilers than a team that wins in January.
swingFactors: Whether any run game emerges behind the line
Takeaway rate regression vs. pressure holding up

bets.reason: The Raiders' 10th-ranked pass offense meets Buffalo's 29th-ranked pass defense, which also ranks 27th on short throws and may be missing slot CB Dee Alford. LV is averaging 26.4 points, Buffalo is allowing 28.2, and Cousins' pass EPA has climbed weekly.
Buffalo's games average 61 combined points (32.8 scored, 28.2 allowed), and the Raiders' last three totaled 62, 57 and 62. Both red-zone defenses rank 27th or worse, and it's indoors.

Net EPA has these teams close (BUF 0.060, 10th; LV 0.034, 12th). Buffalo's point differential is only +4.6 a game, built partly on a 0.75 one-score win rate. The Raiders get home field, a pass-rush edge and a Buffalo offense that turns it over.

confidence.note: Five games, first-year coach, and early-season schedule strength skews the defensive numbers.
